# Bundled data

## stars.json — Yale Bright Star Catalogue, 5th edition

The stars the Planetarium chart draws. 8404 entries down to magnitude 6.5, with
198 carrying a proper name for labelling.

* Source: <http://tdc-www.harvard.edu/catalogs/bsc5.dat.gz> (BSC5, Hoffleit &
  Warren, Astronomical Data Center)
* Generated: 2026-09-09 by `tools/build_star_catalog.py`
* Fields, per row: `[ra, dec, mag, bv, proper, designation]` — RA and Dec are
  J2000 **degrees**, rows sorted brightest first so the renderer can stop early
  at its limiting magnitude and so labels win ties by brightness.

Regenerate with:

    python tools/build_star_catalog.py

That is the only step that needs an internet connection, and the result is
committed. Positions were checked against known J2000 coordinates for ten bright
stars and agree to better than 6 arcseconds.

## milkyway.png — the Milky Way backdrop

The diffuse glow the Planetarium draws behind the stars: the ESO/S. Brunier
360-degree panorama (eso0932a) reduced to half a degree per pixel (720 × 360),
colour kept, with the stars removed by a block median so only the clouds and
dust lanes remain. Galactic coordinates, equirectangular, the centre in the
middle and longitude increasing to the left.

* Source: <https://www.eso.org/public/images/eso0932a/> — credit **ESO/S.
  Brunier**, licence CC BY 4.0. The credit is shown on the Planetarium tab.
* Generated by `tools/build_milky_way.py` (needs Pillow and the source JPEG;
  fetched on first run if not given). The result is committed.

### Why the chart is drawn locally

The Planetarium originally embedded Aladin Lite and streamed HiPS survey imagery
from CDS Strasbourg. That is a 1.8 MB script plus continuous tile downloads:
fine in a browser, but the Edge WebView2 control the desktop window uses took ten
to twenty seconds over the script and sometimes failed outright, which surfaced
as "the sky atlas could not be loaded". A capture PC also routinely sits on a
slow or absent link at a dark site — the worst possible place to depend on a CDN.

Rendering the chart ourselves from this catalogue removes the dependency
entirely: the Planetarium opens instantly and works with the network unplugged,
which is what an observing tool should do. It also matches what Cartes du Ciel
actually shows, which is a vector chart rather than photographs.
